blocks.x: La Bola Negra Review: Sprawling Epic Builds To An Extraordinary Finale [TIFF]
La Bola Negra is an ambitious, sprawling epic that takes its time, but its magnificent final act delivers a deeply moving story of identity.
Published Sep 19, 2026, 5:11 AM EDT

Josh is a film critic and journalist with over nine years of experience in the entertainment industry. Entering the field at just 17 years old, Josh went on to make his own website, The HoloFiles, and social media brand Star Wars Holocron, the most followed Star Wars fan account on Twitter/X.
A member of both the Chicago Indie Critics and the Hollywood Critics Alliance, Josh has covered major industry events including Star Wars Celebration and, most recently, CinemaCon for ScreenRant. His work has appeared in outlets such as Game Rant and Comic Book Resources (CBR), and he has been featured in publications including the BBC and The New York Times.

Unlike some other festivals, it is not often that a Toronto International Film Festival audience erupts into a genuine, lasting standing ovation, but that was the rousing reaction to La bola negra following its Canadian premiere. The film received the kind of sustained, emotional response that suggests it connects to something deeply personal.

Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s sprawling romantic epic is an undeniably ambitious piece of filmmaking. At its best, La bola negra is beautiful, devastating, joyous, and profoundly empathetic, championing the importance of accepting one’s true self. Its ambition also occasionally works against it, taking a winding route toward an admittedly extraordinary destination.

Set across nearly a century, La bola negra follows three gay Spanish men whose lives, romances, losses, and discoveries ultimately become intertwined. The first story chronologically takes place in 1932, when Carlos (Milo Queifes) faces rejection from becoming a member of a local casino community because of rumors that he is gay. Six years later, during the Spanish Civil War, Sebastian (Guitarricadelafuente) is left searching for connection after losing his family.

Decades later, in 2017, Alberto (Carlos González) begins investigating the life of his grandfather after his death, eventually becoming consumed by the mystery surrounding a long-lost stage play. Although these stories initially seem separated by time, geography, and circumstance, each gradually reveals itself as another piece in a larger generational story about sexuality, repression, love, grief, and the consequences of hiding one's identity.
La Bola Negra Tells A Beautiful Story That Takes Quite A While To Arrive

With an extensive runtime of 155 minutes, La bola negra is somewhat of an unwieldy beast for the Javis to wrangle. The runtime would be easier to justify if the sprawling first two acts moved with greater focus, but the film repeatedly stops and starts as it introduces new characters, conflicts, historical circumstances, and emotional developments. There is so much material here that the narrative can occasionally feel disconnected, overdrawn, and unfocused.

A tighter edit could have helped immensely. The film clearly knows where it wants to go, but it takes an unusually long time to get there. Some of the material involving Carlos and Alberto captures one's attention, and the former's storyline eventually produces some particularly gut-wrenching moments, but neither section consistently possesses the same electricity as Sebastian's.

Once Sebastian enters the picture, La bola negra begins to feel considerably more alive. His passion for music, his attempts to conceal both his sexuality and his grief, and his decision to pretend to be a soldier during the Spanish Civil War create an especially compelling portrait of a young man performing a version of himself for a society that would otherwise reject him. His fascination with a captured enemy soldier develops into an unexpected (and refreshingly understated) romance that fundamentally alters the course of his life and, eventually, the lives of people generations removed from him.
The remarkable thing about La bola negra is just how completely and perfectly its myriad of moving parts eventually connect.

The film's structure can therefore be quite the test of patience. Although it is clear that these disparate pieces will eventually connect into a cohesive picture, the build-up is far too extensive for its own good. Thankfully, that changes dramatically once the third act arrives.
La Bola Negra Is Saved By Its Magnificent Final Act
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/lbn_20250828_0439_carlaoset_r2.webp?q=49&fit=crop&w=1300&dpr=2

The remarkable thing about La bola negra is just how completely and perfectly its myriad of moving parts eventually connect. It’s very much akin to a puzzle, pulling itself together from a pile of pieces so disparate that the final picture was difficult to envision.

The third act takes the sprawling narrative that preceded it and suddenly makes sense of why all these seemingly disconnected stories needed to exist. The result is one of the year's most powerful stretches of filmmaking (and one of the best queer stories ever told), transforming the film into something considerably greater than the sum of its parts and making it shockingly easy to overlook the disconnectedness of the first two-thirds.

In chronicling the discovery, development, and eventual dissemination of a stage play about the importance of living authentically, Ambrossi and Calvo essentially create the very piece of art their characters have spent decades trying to preserve. It is a clever, almost meta piece of filmmaking, and such an emotionally satisfying idea, allowing the film's themes of identity and self-acceptance to transcend the story.

And then the emotional barrage begins. The third act contains a whopping number of gut-wrenching lines, revelations, and moments, with the film moving effortlessly between heartbreak and inspiration. A non-queer viewer may come away from La bola negra with a greater understanding of the humanity, fear, and horror experienced by queer people – to quote It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia, this movie could be an “I get it now” moment for many viewers. Meanwhile, queer audiences may find themselves reflected in the film’s characters in ways they never have before.

blocks.x: The film's relationship with history is somewhat more complicated. Its Spanish Civil War sections provide some of its most interesting and emotionally resonant material, but La bola negra occasionally skirts a deeper engagement with the mechanics of rising fascism and the political forces shaping these characters' lives. The historical backdrop is undeniably important, yet the film is ultimately more interested in the intimate consequences of repression than in fully examining the systems producing it.

This prioritization can make the generational trauma feel somewhat isolated by the time the story reaches its modern timeline. The connections across decades are powerful on an emotional level, but the broader historical consequences sometimes feel less accessible than they might have been. Ironically, this also makes the historical sections far more interesting than the Alberto material in 2017, in particular, because the combination of personal repression, romance, and a society undergoing profound political upheaval gives those sequences a sense of urgency that some of the modern-day, slower-paced scenes lacks.

Still, it is difficult to deny the lasting impression La bola negra leaves behind. Younger audiences in particular may find something invaluable in its insistence that identity should not be treated as something to hide or apologize for. Regardless of sexual orientation, the film encourages viewers to live on their own terms and approach the experiences of others with greater empathy and sensitivity. The 155-minute journey may be sprawling, occasionally clunky, and in need of a sharper edit – but its final destination is so profoundly moving that it renders this new film one of the year’s best.
La bola negra screened at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. The film releases in limited US theaters on October 16, before becoming available to stream on Netflix from December 2.
